conventions.convention: For finite graph families, “free” means free of induced copies; complements retain the same vertex set.
$H^+$ adds a vertex adjacent exactly to the two distinguished vertices and makes the distinguished pair adjacent; $H^-$ instead makes that pair nonadjacent.
A $c$-restricted set is a $c$-sparse or $c$-dense nonempty induced vertex set, with the dense count excluding the vertex itself.
$A_{TM}$ and $HALT_{TM}$ consist only of valid encoded machine/input pairs using the stated self-delimiting word code; malformed binary words are not members.
Recognizers accept exactly the positive instances and may diverge on negative ones; deciders additionally halt on every input.
An asymptotic $O(g(n))$ bound holds only beyond a threshold $n_0$, so it supplies no exact bound at every small input length.
NP is defined by polynomial-time verification with polynomially bounded binary certificates, and coNP takes complements inside the same binary ambient language.

$A
	ext{≤}_p B$ is witnessed by a total polynomial-time map with $x
	ext{∈}A$ iff $f(x)
	ext{∈}B$; thus P, NP, and coNP membership transfer from target to source.

load_bearing.statement: Under its stated anticonnected-block, mixedness, and complete-or-mutually-$\eta$-sparse hypotheses, cliques and sufficiently small indexed induced patterns in the auxiliary graph lift to induced ambient patterns; an adjacent distinguished pattern lifts to $H^+$ under the stricter bound.
Under either stated star-subdivision or special-vertex obstruction hypothesis, the auxiliary graph $J$ has a clique or stable set of size at least $|J|^c$ for some $c\in(0,1)$.
Under its equal-block complete-or-mutually-$y^a$-sparse hypotheses and $a\ge 5/c+1$, a clique or stable set of size at least $|I|^c$ in $J$ yields a $y^4$-restricted union of whole blocks.
If a finite family satisfies either stated obstruction hypothesis, then that family is wonderful.

A hypothetical decider for $A_{TM}$ yields a deterministic one-tape machine $D_H$ such that $D_H$ accepts $\overline{\ulcorner M\urcorner}$ iff $M$ does not accept $\overline{\ulcorner M\urcorner}$ for every coded machine $M$ whose input alphabet contains $\Sigma_2$.
The language $HALT_{TM}$ is recognizable but not decidable.
A verifier for $L$ is a polynomial-time decidable binary relation with a polynomial certificate bound, satisfying $x\in L$ iff it has a bounded accepted certificate.
If $A\le_p B$, then $B\in P$ implies $A\in P$, $B\in NP$ implies $A\in NP$, and $B\in coNP$ implies $A\in coNP$.

concerns.concern: [L1] states without qualifications that an induced copy in $J$ lifts block-by-block and that an $H$ copy lifts to $H^+$. The cited lifting lemma requires, respectively, $(q-1)\eta<1$ and $(q-1)\eta<\tfrac12$, and its stated form uses an indexed copy. Although step 2.2 later derives the inequalities in the applications, [L1] itself is an overstrong, unfaithful cited fact.

Step 2.1 says [L3] implies a uniform bound $|\ulcorner P_n\urcorner|\le a+b|\operatorname{bin}(n)|$. [L3] only says the code records a finite transition table; it supplies no compiler-length estimate. For the displayed raw transition-table encoding, the straightforward hard-wired-digit construction uses state references whose code cost is not established as linear in the digit length. The required eventual-size conclusion would follow from an explicit sublinear-in-$n$ compiler bound, but that bound is not proved here.

Step 1.1 applies [L2] with $M=D_H$, but [L2] quantifies over coded machines whereas the diagonal lemma only asserts the existence of a deterministic one-tape machine $D_H$. [L3] guarantees a code only for a machine already presented as coded. A one-line normalization/coding argument for the constructed finite machine is needed before writing $\ulcorner D_H\urcorner$.

Step 1.2 turns the asymptotic assertion that every branch halts within $O(n^k)$ into an exact all-$n$ bound $cn^k$. The library's $O$ convention applies only for $n\ge n_0$, and since $0\in\mathbb N$, the asserted exact bound need not hold at $n=0$. Handling finitely many short lengths or using $c(n+1)^k$ closes the gap.

[L1] attributes the implication from $0<|N_G(v)\cap B_i|<|B_i|$ to “$v$ is mixed on $B_i$” to the cited mixed-anticonnected lemma. That lemma starts after mixedness is assumed; the preliminary implication instead follows immediately from the complete/anticomplete definition for the singleton pair $\{v\},B_i$.
